title: Introduction to DBMS
definition_text:
A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that allows users and applications to create, store, organize, retrieve, update and manage data in a database.

It acts as an interface between users and the database. When a user requests information, the DBMS processes that request, communicates with the database and returns the required result.

A DBMS also provides important facilities such as data security, access control, data integrity, backup and recovery, and transaction management. These facilities help ensure that data remains accurate, protected and available to authorized users.

Examples of DBMS software include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database and SQLite.

summary: Trace the evolution from 1960s Hierarchical and Network models to Codd’s Relational Model and modern Cloud/NoSQL systems.
definition_text: DBMS technology includes 1960s navigational systems such as hierarchical IMS and network-model systems, followed by E. F. Codd’s 1970 relational model. SQL was developed later in the 1970s, followed by object-relational, NoSQL, and distributed cloud systems; these models have coexisted.

definition_text: Organizations need a DBMS because manual file code breaks down when data grows beyond memory, when hundreds of users edit simultaneously, when queries change unexpectedly (ad-hoc queries), or when sudden crashes threaten partial writes.

summary: Distinguish DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, and TCL command groups in SQL.
definition_text: DQL / DML / DDL: In this course convention, DQL queries rows (SELECT); DML modifies rows (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE); and DDL defines structures (CREATE/ALTER/DROP). Some sources group SELECT under DML instead. This course uses a common teaching classification: DQL (SELECT) reads data; DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) changes rows; DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) defines structures; DCL (GRANT, REVOKE) controls permissions; and TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK) manages transactions. Textbooks and vendors do not all separate DQL from DML; some classify SELECT as part of DML, so follow the convention stated by the course or exam.

title: SQL EXISTS

definition_text: Second Normal Form (2NF): 1NF relation where no non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key. title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
summary: Enforce the strictest determinant rule: for every non-trivial X -> Y, X MUST be a Superkey.
definition_text: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF): Strict normal form requiring every non-trivial determinant X (in X -> Y) to be a Superkey. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) strengthens 3NF with one crisp rule: for EVERY non-trivial functional dependency `X -> Y` holding in relation `R`, `X` MUST be a Superkey of `R`. Every BCNF table is guaranteed to be in 3NF, though a few 3NF schemas violate BCNF when overlapping candidate keys exist.
example_text: Consider `R(student_id, instructor_id, course_id)` with `instructor_id -> course_id`, while instructors may have many students. Then `instructor_id` does not identify every row, so this non-trivial dependency violates BCNF. Decompose into `InstructorCourse(instructor_id, course_id)` and `StudentInstructor(student_id, instructor_id)` under these stated dependencies. Example: SELECT instructor_id, full_name, dept_id FROM instructors;
